The threespot damselfish Stegastes planifrons is a common inhabitant of Caribbean coral reefs, where it maintains algal gardens that are defended vigorously against herbivorous intruders. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal nests after a brief embryonic period; at a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], eclosion occurs approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days] after oviposition, a duration consistent with the rapid developmental rates reported for other pomacentrids under similar thermal regimes. The minute prolarvae that exit the chorion are lecithotrophic, possessing a substantial yolk sac that sustains them through the initial non-feeding interval. These early-stage larvae are extremely small, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter for this species and reflecting the considerable energetic constraints of producing large numbers of such diminutive offspring across multiple spawning events throughout the reproductive season.

As the larvae progress through the pelagic larval phase, they undergo a suite of morphological transformations culminating in metamorphosis and settlement onto reef habitat. The transition from the planktonic to the benthic environment marks a critical juncture in the species' life history, after which juvenile growth proceeds rapidly. Field surveys of newly settled juveniles indicate that puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and the first detectable vitellogenic activity in the ovaries, is attained at a relatively modest standard length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters]. This size corresponds to a calculated wet weight of 5.4 grams [Wwp = 5.4 grams], which represents approximately one-sixth of the ultimate wet mass achieved by fully grown adults. The achievement of this body size typically occurs within the first year of benthic life, although local variation in food availability and intra-specific competition for high-quality algal territories can delay maturation in some individuals, a pattern observed in many congeneric damselfishes.

Adult threespot damselfish continue to grow after sexual maturation, albeit at a decelerated rate, until they approach an asymptotic size that defines the species' maximum body dimensions. Extensive sampling across multiple reef sites throughout the greater Caribbean demonstrates that the ultimate standard length rarely exceeds 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], placing Stegastes planifrons among the mid-sized members of its genus. The corresponding asymptotic body mass, derived from the length-weight relationship obtained from over two hundred dissected specimens, is 32 grams [Wwi = 32 grams]. This adult body size is functionally linked to the species' territorial behavior; larger individuals are capable of defending higher-quality algal mats that support greater reproductive output, though the energetic demands of constant patrolling and nest preparation also increase with body mass. Comparative studies show that the ultimate length of S. planifrons is intermediate between that of the smaller dusky damselfish Stegastes adustus and the larger beaugregory Stegastes leucostictus.

Reproductive activity in Stegastes planifrons is tightly coupled to water temperature and peaks during the warm summer months when surface waters approach 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. Under these optimal thermal conditions, nesting males prepare and defend a demersal spawning site, typically a flat rock surface cleared of algae, to which females are attracted for oviposition. Data from controlled laboratory observations conducted at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] indicate that a reproductively active female can sustain a maximum daily egg production of 125 eggs per day [Ri = 125 eggs per day]. This elevated rate is comparable to that estimated for the congeneric Chromis chromis under similar thermal conditions and reflects the iteroparous strategy of the species, wherein females produce many small clutches sequentially over the course of a protracted spawning season, rather than one or two large annual batches.

Longevity data for the threespot damselfish, compiled from mark-recapture studies conducted on a protected reef in the Florida Keys, reveal that individuals can attain a considerable lifespan for such a small-bodied teleost. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the region at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan reaches 6935 days [am = 6935 days], which is equivalent to approximately 19 years. This extended life expectancy, which approaches two decades, is notable among damselfishes and is likely facilitated by the species' aggressive defense of a high-quality food resource that buffers individuals against seasonal fluctuations in planktonic prey availability. The combination of a long lifespan with a high, sustained daily reproductive output results in a life-history strategy that is heavily weighted toward repeated breeding over many years, contrasting sharply with the semelparous or short-lived strategies adopted by many other small-bodied reef fishes occupying less stable microhabitats.
